prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned prose, centred on a large novelistic oeuvre and grounded in Romanian poetry, in which memory, the body and dream are built into an encyclopedic metaphysical cosmos

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in the writer and alternatives, and I have adjusted the citation. No new evidence has entered the exchange, and I will not move a first preference only because the opening count is split. Cărtărescu remains my choice on the common criteria. The voice is one I would not mistake for another writer's: dense, patterned prose in which body, childhood memory, dream and metaphysical speculation form a single imaginative substance. The Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid show formal ambition at very large scale, and they vary register from the intimate to the cosmic while keeping one identity. The career runs over several decades from a poetic beginning, which bears on maturity. The intellectual depth lies in recasting a Romantic and modernist inheritance as a personal cosmology. I take Sem-Sandberg's point about scope and now centre the citation on the novels, with the poetry named as ground and not as an equal pillar, because I know the poetry least well and the novels are where the claim is best supported. A single-writer citation fits, since the contribution is a body of work and not one title. This remains a close call against Can Xue, and I hold it as a judgment from public knowledge and translations, not as a verified finding.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. Very long, ornate books may repeat motif in ways that are exhaustion and not architecture, and I cannot show from public knowledge that the density holds at the same level in every volume. Olsson's question about originality beyond the lineage is also still open for some colleagues. My answer, that the inheritance is transformed into a synthesis found nowhere else, is a reading and not a demonstration. The judgment is mediated by translation, and the poetry and earlier prose are thinly covered, so the claimed unity of prose and poetry is partly inferred. Can Xue's formal discipline is a serious rival, and Carlberg, Palm and Swärd argue forcefully that rigour of method is a stronger sign of sustained quality than scale. If the committee's reading across the later long books shows thinning in Cărtărescu, or real variation within Can Xue's method, I would move Can Xue to first. Neither has been shown in the exchange.

responses.point: Swärd holds that a single stable method held with rigour is a stronger sign of sustained quality than scale alone. She would reconsider the order of Can Xue and Cărtărescu if colleagues can show real variation within the method.
responses.response: I take the principle seriously, because scale is not quality and I do not want to argue that it is. I would turn the test around. Rigour of method counts as sustained quality only if the method keeps finding new material, and Swärd concedes she cannot yet show that for Can Xue. I make the same concession for Cărtărescu's late volumes. So the principle favours neither of us until someone has read across the later work of both. For me, a visionary prose that keeps widening its field while keeping its identity shows rigour of another kind. That is a judgment I hold provisionally, and it could reasonably go her way.

responses.point: Palm argues that in Can Xue the variety lies in invention within each work and not in a change of method. She adds that the compression of the work makes repetition cost less than in Cărtărescu's long books.
responses.response: The compression point is real. Repetition in a short story and repetition across a thousand pages do not cost the same, and I accept that this is a genuine asymmetry in Can Xue's favour. I would still say that compression does not by itself answer the sustained-quality question. It moves the question to the novels, where Carlberg and Swärd already ask whether the long works hold up as well as the stories. Palm admits she cannot settle this from the corpus, and neither can I. I therefore do not treat the asymmetry as decisive. It is a reason to keep Can Xue as my first alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg shares my first preference but argues that coherence across prose and poetry should not be credited from the major novels alone. He would accept a citation with the novels at the centre and the poetry as foundation.
responses.response: I accept this and have revised my citation. My round-1 wording gave the poetry more weight than my knowledge of it supports. Coverage of the poems in translation is thin, and I should not credit the whole body of work with a unity I have seen mainly in the novels. The revised citation names the novels as the centre and the poetry as ground. I also agree that our shared first place is not a literary argument and should not be counted as one. I would still want the committee to test the late long volumes on the page, which is the point on which he and I agree.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita first and finds his sequences more tightly built than a novelist's cycle. He remains unsure whether Cărtărescu's originality goes beyond the lineage he draws on, and he asks that each section of a long work earn its length.
responses.response: I accept the test that each section must earn its length, and I apply it to Cărtărescu without exemption. Olsson says his own reading of the novels is only in translation, and mine is too, so the test cannot be closed by either of us. On Zurita, I still cannot let the case move forward unless it rests on the verbal achievement of the sequences. The chair says he accepts that condition, and I take that seriously. Carlberg, Palm, Sem-Sandberg and Swärd say they need Spanish-language expert input to be persuaded. I would want that input before I could place Zurita above the two fiction writers. Until then I keep him outside my alternatives. The reason is my uncertainty about judging poetry in translation, not any doubt about the seriousness of the project.

responses.point: Carlberg judges that Can Xue's formal discipline appears to be the work itself, while Cărtărescu's achievement leans more on accumulation and lineage. She says she would not resist a committee reading that rates his long novels higher.
responses.response: I find the distinction between discipline as the work itself and accumulation useful, though I would not accept that accumulation is a lesser mode. In a cycle like the Blinding trilogy, accumulation is the formal principle, and the question is whether it is controlled. Carlberg says she would not resist a reading that rates the long novels higher, and I note that. I read it as an openness and not as agreement, since her own ranking still puts Cărtărescu third. I cannot answer her lineage worry beyond what I said earlier: the test is whether the inheritance becomes a voice found nowhere else.

uncertainties: My knowledge rests on public information and translations, not on independent verification. I cannot judge the Romanian original, and the effect of long, ornate sentences in translation is uncertain.

Whether Cărtărescu's later long volumes extend the earlier project or restate it cannot be settled from the supplied evidence. I can name only the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid with confidence and cannot point to specific later works that show development.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and earlier prose is thin, so the claim of a unified project across poetry and prose is partly inferred. This is why the revised citation centres the novels.
The Can Xue versus Cărtărescu comparison turns on how much variation each oeuvre shows. It is a close judgment that could go either way, and the available evidence does not decide it.
Poetry in translation (Zurita, Adonis) and hybrid work (Carson) cannot be compared with the novelists on an equal footing without regional expert input that is not part of the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. I update my round-1 note on one point. My own novel Den svarta månens år is described as a dream-logic novel, and Can Xue's method is also dream logic. I record this as a proximity of practice for others to weigh, and it is not a documented connection to either writer. My practice is context and is not evidence that I favour Cărtărescu or Can Xue. My ties to committee colleagues, including my joint entry to the committee with Swärd, are context only. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
